author: reek
body: An Interval is the set of signed 64-bit integers { v : lo <= v <= hi } with INCLUSIVE endpoints. The full i64 range is the "unknown" interval: it is always a sound answer, and every transfer function returns it whenever an endpoint computation would overflow i64. The kernel proves containment only - no relational facts, no strides, no known bits; the full list of what it deliberately does not do is in the Limitations section at the end.

author: reek
body: Two distinguished values. iv-unknown is the full i64 range, the sound answer of last resort. iv-empty is the empty interval - the witness that no value can flow, produced by intersecting disjoint ranges. Empty is represented by lo > hi, tested by iv-is-empty, and every function in this chapter that produces an empty result returns the one canonical value iv-empty, never any other lo > hi pair. Returning iv-unknown for an empty intersection would be sound but lossy; the distinguished empty is one comparison and keeps dead-branch facts exact. A transfer function handed an empty operand returns iv-empty: the soundness contracts below quantify over the concrete members of the inputs, and an empty input has none, so the empty result is vacuously sound and maximally precise.

author: reek
body: The i64 endpoint constants. The compiler defines i64-min and i64-max in the Codex Types chapter, but this chapter must stand alone for consumers that cite only the kernel, and redefining those names here would collide in the self-compile unit, so the kernel carries its own prefixed copies.

author: reek
body: SOUNDNESS CONTRACT: for every concrete pair (x, y) with x in the input's range and y in the other input's range, the concrete result x + y lies inside the returned interval. Addition is monotone in both arguments, so the exact bounds are the endpoint sums; if either endpoint sum would overflow i64, the answer is iv-unknown, which is always sound.

author: reek
body: SOUNDNESS CONTRACT: for every concrete pair (x, y) with x in the input's range and y in the other input's range, the concrete result x - y lies inside the returned interval. Subtraction is monotone up in the left argument and monotone down in the right, so the exact bounds are lo = a.lo - b.hi and hi = a.hi - b.lo; if either would overflow i64, the answer is iv-unknown.

author: reek
body: SOUNDNESS CONTRACT: for every concrete x in the input's range, the concrete result 0 - x lies inside the returned interval. Negation swaps and negates the endpoints exactly, except that negating iv-i64-min overflows, so any interval containing it answers iv-unknown.

author: reek
body: SOUNDNESS CONTRACT: for every concrete pair (x, y) with x in the input's range and y in the other input's range, the concrete result x * y lies inside the returned interval. For fixed x the product is monotone in y (direction given by the sign of x) and symmetrically for fixed y, so over the input box the extremes are attained at the four corners; the result is the min and max of the four corner products. If any corner product would overflow i64, the answer is iv-unknown.

author: reek
body: SOUNDNESS CONTRACT: for every concrete pair (x, y) with x in the input's range, y in the other input's range, and y not zero, the concrete result x / y lies inside the returned interval. Codex division truncates toward zero (idiv), and truncating division is monotone in the dividend for a fixed divisor and monotone in the divisor over a divisor range of fixed sign, so the extremes over the box are attained at the four corners. A divisor range containing zero answers iv-unknown: the range still holds nonzero divisors whose quotients must be contained, and unknown contains them all. The single overflowing corner, iv-i64-min divided by -1, also answers iv-unknown; a negative divisor range contains -1 exactly when its high endpoint is -1.

author: reek
body: SOUNDNESS CONTRACT: every concrete x in either input's range lies inside the returned interval. The result is the convex hull - the gap between disjoint inputs is included, because an interval cannot represent it. An empty side contributes nothing and the other side is returned unchanged. No overflow is possible: the result endpoints are copies of input endpoints.

author: reek
body: SOUNDNESS CONTRACT: for every concrete pair (x, y) with x in the input's range and y in the other input's range, the concrete result min(x, y) lies inside the returned interval - and symmetrically for max. min(x, y) is at least the smaller lo and at most the smaller hi (it is bounded above by both x and y separately); max mirrors the argument with the larger endpoints. Both are exact and cannot overflow.

author: reek
body: What this kernel provably does not do, so nobody rediscovers the gaps the hard way.

author: reek
body: It carries no relational facts: it cannot express i != j, x < y, or any link between two expressions - each interval is an independent fact about one value. It carries no stride or congruence information (an interval of even numbers is indistinguishable from its hull) and no known-bits domain. It refuses to iv-unknown whenever ANY endpoint computation would overflow i64; there are no wrapping intervals, so a sum that overflows loses everything, not just the overflowing end. Division and modulo refuse the whole answer when the divisor range merely CONTAINS zero - no splitting of a mixed-sign divisor range around zero is attempted. The modulo bound is magnitude-only, [0, max abs(divisor) - 1]: it does not exploit the dividend at all, so int-mod of a small non-negative dividend by a large divisor is not recognized as the dividend itself. Union returns the convex hull, losing any gap between disjoint inputs. And the empty interval is a single canonical witness, not a representation of arbitrary empty sets: consumers must test with iv-is-empty, never compare endpoints of an empty result.
